assessment.nobel_worthiness: The firm-heterogeneity framework changed how trade is modelled. It explains selection into exporting, within-industry reallocation and the gains from trade. It has generated a large body of testable predictions and a shared empirical toolkit, and it is used in policy evaluation.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central, clearly identifiable contribution. Helpman's work on trade with differentiated products and his firm-level extensions (including with Melitz and Yeaple) make him a natural second laureate. Redding is a significant later contributor, but his credit is less clearly separable at this stage. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen, Kortum and others sit outside this ballot entry and complicate the attribution.
assessment.maturity: Over two decades of replication, extension and empirical testing across many countries and datasets. The core predictions have held up reasonably well, which makes this a mature and robust body of work.
uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers to credit the empirical firm-level trade literature (Bernard, Jensen and others) alongside the theory.
Helpman is also credited on a separate ballot entry, which may create overlap.
Some structural results depend on functional-form assumptions, such as Pareto productivity.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Collateral constraints and the financial accelerator explain how small shocks are amplified through credit markets. This became the standard framework for thinking about credit cycles and financial frictions in macroeconomics. It had major influence on post-2008 research and policy thinking.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki-Moore (1997) and the Bernanke-Gertler line of work are the core. Bernanke is not on this ballot, and he already shares the 2022 prize for work on banks and financial crises. Gilchrist is a significant empirical contributor but less central. Gertler's later work on banking and unconventional policy strengthens his case.
assessment.maturity: Foundational papers date from the 1990s, with long confirmation through empirical work and use in the financial-crisis literature. The framework is widely adopted.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises, which may be seen as reducing novelty.
Gertler is also credited in the New Keynesian ballot entry.
Direct empirical identification of collateral channels is harder than the theory's influence suggests.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: This work documented the labour-market consequences of trade exposure and technological change, with persistent regional and worker-level effects. It also brought task-based thinking into the empirics of wage inequality. It had large influence on policy debate and shifted professional beliefs about adjustment costs.
assessment.attribution: The China-shock papers are clearly credited to Autor, Dorn and Hanson, and Autor is the common thread through the task-based work as well. Dorn is a junior co-author on the trade-shock papers. Katz's contributions on skill demand are substantial but partly overlap with prior recognition of related work (Goldin 2023; Acemoglu 2024).
assessment.maturity: The main results date from roughly 2013-2016 and have been replicated and extended with several datasets. Debate about magnitudes and mechanisms continues, which is normal for a policy-relevant literature.
uncertainties: Sensitivity of the estimates to the shift-share identification strategy and instrument design.
Contested interpretation of magnitudes and long-run adjustment.
Choice among Autor, Hanson, Dorn and Katz.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: This work formalised how electoral rules, constitutions and state capacity shape fiscal and policy outcomes, and it set an agenda for political economics. It combines rigorous theory with empirical tests, notably comparisons of electoral systems and studies of fiscal capacity.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the clearest co-originators through their joint research program and book. Besley's contributions on state capacity, accountability and development are substantial and partly independent. Other important contributors are not on the ballot.
assessment.maturity: More than 25 years of development with extensive follow-up empirical work. Some causal claims about electoral rules have been refined or qualified over time.
uncertainties: Whether the empirical constitutional-effects results are robust under modern credibility standards.
Overlap with the 2024 recognition of institutions and prosperity (Acemoglu, Johnson, Robinson).
The three-person limit and how to treat Besley's separate contributions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: This work measures intergenerational mobility using population administrative data and exploits quasi-experiments to identify neighbourhood effects. It changed the empirical standard in public economics and enabled policy-relevant, transparent measurement at scale.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the central figure and leads the program. Hendren is credited for the neighbourhood-effects and exposure-effects work. Friedman and Katz are important co-authors, but the credit is spread across a large team. Attribution within large collaborations carries real uncertainty.
assessment.maturity: The main papers date from about 2014 to 2022. The datasets are public and some results have been replicated, but long-run confirmation of the neighbourhood-causal estimates is still developing.
uncertainties: Maturity: the causal neighbourhood-effect estimates are recent, and some are contested on methodological grounds.
Chetty's work also appears on the optimal-taxation ballot, so a laureate choice here interacts with that entry.
How the committee weighs team science and data access against individual attribution.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Fairness, reciprocity and inequity-aversion models gave behavioural economics a tractable theory of social preferences. Experiments tested it directly, and the work shaped contract theory, public goods, institutions and labour markets. This line of work also showed that careful experimental design can discriminate between competing models.
assessment.attribution: Fehr-Schmidt (1999) is the core theory contribution, and Fehr's experimental program on punishment and reciprocity is broad. Falk's contributions on reciprocity, preferences and field evidence are substantial. Rabin, Bolton-Ockenfels and others are outside the ballot entry, so attribution is contested.
assessment.maturity: More than 25 years of replication and extension. The core qualitative regularities (reciprocity, costly punishment, inequity aversion) are robust in many large-scale replications. Some specific strong-reciprocity claims and generalisability from the lab to field behaviour are debated.
uncertainties: Contested priority and attribution relative to Rabin, Bolton and Ockenfels.
External validity of lab measures of social preferences.
I have professional proximity to this literature through experimental and replication work, so I have tried to apply the same criteria as for other fields.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The law-and-finance program showed that legal institutions and investor protection are systematically related to financial development and corporate governance. It opened a large empirical research agenda and influenced policy debate on institutional reform.
assessment.attribution: The core 1990s papers are by La Porta, Lopez-de-Silanes, Shleifer and Vishny. A three-laureate limit forces a choice, and Vishny's separate contributions to corporate governance and behavioural finance complicate the picture. Shleifer's very wide influence across fields also makes attribution to this specific theme less clean.
assessment.maturity: Highly cited and long established. However, the legal-origins hypothesis has faced substantial criticism on measurement, causal identification and robustness, and the evidence for it is weaker than its influence suggests.
uncertainties: Robustness and causal interpretation of legal-origins and anti-director-rights indices.
Concerns about measurement and coding choices in the original datasets.
Choice among the four credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Partial identification provides a principled way to report what data can support under weak, credible assumptions. It is a methodological contribution that applies across fields and addresses the problem of overconfident inference. The framework supports honest uncertainty reporting in empirical work.
assessment.attribution: Manski is the founder of the approach (bounds, identification problems). Tamer is a leading contributor on moment inequalities and set inference in structural models. Molinari has made major contributions to inference and applications. The attribution is clear for Manski but less so beyond him.
assessment.maturity: More than 30 years of development, with a mature inference theory. Adoption in applied work has been gradual and uneven, which tempers evidence of broad practical impact.
uncertainties: Breadth of applied adoption relative to other econometric methods.
How the committee weighs foundational but less widely used methodology against applied-impact candidates.
Choice among Manski, Tamer and Molinari.
